title: India's Sweeping Food Safety Crackdown Hits Quick Commerce Giants and Liquor Makers
excerpt: Maharashtra's food safety chief has suspended permits at Blinkit, Swiggy, and Zepto warehouses while FSSAI bans popular Diageo and Inbrew spirits for artificial flavouring, marking India's most aggressive enforcement push in years.
body:
• Maharashtra food safety chief Tukaram Mundhe has suspended permits of 12 warehouses of Blinkit, Swiggy Instamart, and Zepto and shut four Domino's outlets for hygiene violations including cockroach infestations
  • FSSAI banned several Diageo and Inbrew whisky and rum brands for using artificial flavouring instead of proper ageing, in what the regulator calls an unprecedented enforcement action
  • Diageo has agreed to reformulate popular brands including Antiquity Blue, Royal Challenge, and McDowell's No. 1 Rum to comply with regulations nationwide
  • The crackdown spans India's $13 billion quick commerce sector and $40 billion alcohol industry, with FSSAI also launching spice surveillance and festival-season drives across all states

India's food safety apparatus has launched its most aggressive enforcement drive in recent memory, with a crusading state official shutting down popular restaurant chains and warehouse operations while the national regulator bans well-known liquor brands for misleading consumers.

Maharashtra's One-Man Cleanup

Tukaram Mundhe, Maharashtra's new food safety chief, has become a household name in India's most populous state after a series of raids that have rattled both legacy eateries and billion-dollar tech-driven delivery companies.

His department suspended the permits of 12 warehouses belonging to India's three largest quick-commerce companies — five operated by Eternal's Blinkit, five by Zepto, and two by Swiggy's Instamart — after inspectors found cockroach infestations, rotten vegetables, rodent droppings, and rusted storage racks, according to Reuters.

The raids have put a spotlight on the $13 billion quick commerce sector, where companies promise grocery deliveries within minutes and collectively clock 9 million daily orders. Blinkit operates roughly 2,200 delivery outlets across India, while Swiggy and Zepto each have about 1,100, according to Datum Intelligence.

Mundhe's team also shut four Domino's outlets in the state — a notable escalation given that the pizza chain, India's biggest fast-food brand, is typically considered to maintain stricter safety protocols than local competitors. In total, Maharashtra's Food and Drug Administration has inspected 86 establishments and issued 60 improvement notices.

Alcohol Industry Under Fire

At the national level, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has turned its attention to the country's $40 billion alcohol market. The regulator banned several whisky and rum brands made by Diageo's Indian subsidiary United Spirits and India's Inbrew Beverages after tests revealed companies were adding artificial flavourings — like rum flavour to rum and whisky flavour to whisky — rather than relying on proper ageing and natural ingredients.

"There is no internationally recognized manufacturing practice whereby rum flavour is added to rum or whisky flavour is added to whisky."

— FSSAI statement on the alcohol industry crackdown

The banned products include some of Diageo's most popular brands in India: Antiquity Blue Whisky and Royal Challenge Whisky produced in Madhya Pradesh, and McDowell's No. 1 Celebration Matured XXX Rum from Maharashtra. Royal Challenge alone sells over 4.5 million nine-litre cases annually in India.

FSSAI also warned Diageo that Royal Challenge's label claim of being "matured in American oak casks" was misleading, since the product's main ingredient after water is grain neutral spirit that has not been matured, Reuters reported.

By mid-August, Diageo agreed to reformulate its affected brands to eliminate the problematic flavourings, according to Reuters, citing government sources. The reformulation requirement applies nationwide, not just in states where sales were initially restricted. FSSAI conditionally lifted the ban, allowing existing stock to be sold with corrected labeling.

Wider Enforcement Push

The crackdown extends beyond Maharashtra and the liquor industry. FSSAI has directed all states to ramp up surveillance of milk, sweets, and dairy products ahead of the festive season, when demand surges and adulteration risks rise. Mobile food-testing units are being deployed to prominent markets, and inspection data must be uploaded to the regulator's digital compliance platforms.

The authority has also launched a nationwide spice surveillance drive, directing states to test samples of 13 spices — including black pepper, turmeric, cumin, and chilli — for contaminants, microbial counts, and labeling compliance. Results are due by November.

Separately, FSSAI has urged consumers to report unsafe food practices through its Food Safety Connect mobile app, signaling a shift toward citizen-driven enforcement alongside traditional inspections.

What It Means for Consumers

For India's 1.4 billion consumers, the enforcement wave marks a departure from years of lax oversight. The quick commerce raids could force structural improvements in how companies store and handle food products at scale. The alcohol industry crackdown may drive up costs for some popular budget whisky and rum brands as manufacturers invest in proper ageing processes rather than synthetic shortcuts.

Whether the momentum sustains remains an open question. India's food safety infrastructure has historically struggled with understaffing and inconsistent enforcement across states. But Mundhe's high-profile approach in Maharashtra, backed by FSSAI's national-level actions, suggests regulators are testing a more aggressive model that could reshape consumer protection across the country.
